p: Alexander had positioned his guns with extraordinary care. They stretched for nearly two miles along Seminary Ridge, wheel to wheel in places, the barrels elevated slightly to reach the distant blue line on Cemetery Ridge. The Washington Artillery of New Orleans — the most famous artillery unit in the Confederate army — was in the line. Pegram's battalion fired from the northern end. Cabell's and Henry's battalions fired from the south.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: On Cemetery Ridge, the Union infantry pressed themselves flat behind the stone walls and into the shallow hollows and swales of the ground. The Confederate fire was intense but, as Hunt had feared, much of it was overshooting — landing behind the ridge near the Taneytown Road, destroying caissons and limbers, killing horses and headquarters staff, nearly hitting Meade himself.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Hunt watched the fire carefully. He began deliberately silencing the Union guns — battery by battery, pulling them back or having them cease fire. He was conserving ammunition for what he knew was coming. Hancock, riding the line and watching his infantry press closer to the ground, overruled him on some batteries: keep firing, he said. The men need to see their guns fighting.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: For nearly two hours the ground shook.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Then Alexander sent his first message to Pickett.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: And then the guns fell silent, and across the open fields of Pennsylvania, 12,500 men in gray and butternut stepped out of the tree line and began to walk east.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Alonzo Cushing was twenty-two years old.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: He had graduated from West Point in 1861 and commanded Battery A, 4th US Artillery — six three-inch rifles positioned directly behind the stone wall at The Angle, at the exact focal point of the Confederate assault.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The cannonade had been brutal for his battery. Horses killed. Men down. Two of his six guns disabled. By the time Pickett's infantry appeared at the tree line, Cushing had four guns serviceable and was wounded himself — a fragment through the shoulder.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: As the Confederate line crossed the Emmitsburg Road and came on, Cushing took another hit. The wound was grave — a shell fragment through the groin. His sergeant, Frederick Fuger, urged him to go to the rear.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Cushing refused. He had two guns left. He would serve them himself.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: With Fuger's help, he moved his last two guns to the wall itself — the stone wall at The Angle — and loaded them with double canister. As Armistead's men climbed over the wall on his left, as the Union line bent and buckled around him, Cushing fired one last round of canister into the Confederate infantry at a range of perhaps twenty yards.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: He was shot through the mouth.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Fuger assumed command of what remained of the battery. The Angle held.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Cushing's family petitioned for a Medal of Honor for the next century and a half. The Army reviewed the case repeatedly. Bureaucratic obstacles — the statute of limitations, administrative requirements — delayed the award for generations.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: On November 6, 2014, President Obama presented the Medal of Honor to a descendant of Cushing's family at a White House ceremony. Alonzo Cushing received the nation's highest military honor 151 years after he died earning it — the longest gap between action and award in the history of the decoration.
